records.name: Connecticut Microgrid Grant and Loan Program (Public Act 12-148 Sec. 7) — the per-site civic-resilience cost dataset
records.what_it_is: Connecticut's post-Irene/Sandy statute directed DEEP to run a microgrid grant and loan programme for critical facilities. A municipality, electric distribution company, municipal electric utility, energy improvement district or private entity applies in a competitive round; DEEP awards a grant or loan and the recipient owns and operates the microgrid, reporting annually to PURA, the Office of Consumer Counsel, DEEP and two legislative committees for five years. The decisive statutory limit is on what the money buys: under the pilot the grants and loans pay only for design, engineering services and interconnection infrastructure — not the generator. A 2016 bond expansion widened this to matching funds or low-interest loans for energy storage and clean distributed generation. DEEP's own award-tracking chart is the per-site dataset: 12 operational microgrids and $22,265,935 of awards.

records.term: Grant or loan; recipient must report project status annually for five years to PURA, OCC, DEEP and the appropriations and energy committees
records.price_form: grant-funded (and low-interest loans), restricted by statute to design, engineering services and interconnection infrastructure

records.nuclear_fit: Admits a reactor by construction — the only mechanism in this file that does. Public Act 12-148 Sec. 7(a)(3) defines the eligible resource purely by size and location: 'the generation of electricity from a unit with a rating of not more than sixty-five megawatts on the premises of a retail end user'. There is no fuel list, no emissions test, no efficiency gate and no renewability requirement — the exact opposite of the PUCT's closed natural-gas-or-propane enumeration and the CPUC's combustion-or-chemical-reaction-and-renewable fuel rule. A 1-20 MW reactor on a hospital or municipal campus satisfies the definition on its face. The statutory 'critical facility' list is equally accommodating: hospital, police station, fire station, water treatment plant, sewage treatment plant, public shelter, correctional facility, any commercial area of a municipality, a municipal centre, or anything else DEEP identifies as critical. The catch is on the money, not the eligibility: the pilot grant may fund only design, engineering services and interconnection infrastructure, so a reactor developer gets its wires and controls paid for and none of its capex.
records.microreactor_edge: Two things. First, the 65 MW statutory ceiling is written as a maximum, so a smaller unit is strictly safer under it while a full-size reactor is excluded outright — this is one of the few rules where being small is legally load-bearing rather than merely commercially convenient. Second, the delivered fleet shows what a reactor would be replacing: ten of the twelve operational Connecticut microgrids are anchored on natural gas CHP, fuel cells or diesel, and the only battery-led project kept a natural gas generator on site anyway. On capacity the fit is direct — the built systems run from about 200 kW to 4.2 MW, so a single unit at the bottom of the microreactor band covers any of them and most of them several times over.
blockers: PA 12-148 Sec. 7(c): grants and loans may only fund design, engineering services and interconnection infrastructure — no generation capex under the pilot authority

records.nuclear_fit: Ignores nuclear — the eligibility rule is about which BUILDINGS are in the cluster, not which machine powers it — and it contains the single most useful regulator finding in this file for a firm non-emitting resource. The Board found that 'existing technology and cost considerations currently do not allow for renewable DERs alone, or renewable DERs coupled with energy storage, to provide the level and length of resilience that critical facilities need' and therefore that 'the inclusion of fossil fueled DER in TCDER Phase II Incentive Program projects is necessary at this time'. Every one of the eight funded designs proves it: each carries natural gas CHP or gas/diesel gensets, and the Board simultaneously URGES awardees to minimise fossil DER. That is a regulator publicly stating a capability gap it cannot close with the technologies on its own list. The gating constraint for a reactor is not eligibility but the applicant's own certification that the project 'is legally permissible' under existing law, code and standing Board Orders — which for a multi-building municipal cluster means crossing public streets, and therefore squarely raises New Jersey's right-of-way question.
records.microreactor_edge: The size match is almost exact and it is measured, not asserted: six of the eight funded designs sit between 1.7 MW and 4.4 MW, and the median awarded project is about 2.5 MW. A single 1-20 MW unit covers any of them, and covers the two 20 MW outliers (Atlantic City, Trenton) as a small fleet. Crucially these are multi-day-outage resilience assets whose fossil DER exists precisely because storage cannot hold the duration — the one attribute a reactor has for free. The programme's own money is far too small (a $196K-$1.1M design grant) to matter, so the value here is the documented demand shape and the named counterparties, not the funding.

records.what_it_is: The host buys the generator outright and uses the output only on its own contiguous property. Because no electricity changes hands, there is no sale, no retail service, and in nearly every state no public-utility status to argue about. The host carries the whole capital cost and the whole performance risk, and gets the whole benefit. This is the only structure that is available in all fifty states without asking anyone's permission.

records.nuclear_fit: This is the cleanest structure for a reactor and the one every early order should assume. A host that owns the reactor and consumes all its output is not selling power, so no PUC has jurisdiction over the transaction — the entire regulatory load falls on the NRC licence and the local AHJ instead of on utility law. The catch is that it requires the host to own a nuclear facility, which means the host, not the vendor, is the NRC licensee and carries decommissioning funding assurance.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1–20 MW unit is small enough that a single campus, mine or terminal can absorb its entire output, which is what makes self-service viable at all. A 300 MW reactor forces its owner to sell the surplus, and the moment it sells, every structure below applies. Sizing the machine to one property's own load is therefore not just an engineering choice — it is what keeps the deal out of utility regulation.

records.name: Resiliency-as-a-Service (RaaS): third-party-owned backup microgrid sold as a monthly subscription
records.what_it_is: The host signs a long-term services agreement with a microgrid developer instead of buying generators. The developer finances, owns, permits, operates and maintains the generating plant on the host's land; the host grants a site licence/easement and pays a one-time set-up fee for construction plus a recurring monthly service fee. Availability and maintenance risk sit with the developer; the host typically pays fuel only during an actual outage. The developer keeps the merchant upside (grid-services and demand-response revenue from the same iron), which is what subsidises the service fee below the cost of owning a diesel fleet.

records.nuclear_fit: The instrument itself is technology-agnostic and is the single closest commercial analogue to selling a reactor as a service: the host never takes title, never operates, and never carries fuel logistics. But three things break for a reactor. (1) The developer-owner must hold the NRC licence and be the operator, so the 'we own and operate it on your land' clause maps to a real NRC 10 CFR 50/52 licensee obligation and a site that is now a licensed nuclear facility with an emergency-planning zone. (2) State retail-sale law: in most regulated states a non-utility selling metered electricity to a host across a property line needs a third-party-sale exemption; RaaS providers avoid this today by selling a *service* (availability) rather than kWh. (3) The merchant upside that subsidises the fee — bidding the asset into demand response and grid services — is exactly what an emergency-only diesel engine cannot do and what a reactor, as a baseload machine, also cannot do well, because a reactor wants to run 24/7 rather than sit idle for 8,700 hours.
records.microreactor_edge: A factory-built 1-20 MW unit fits the RaaS balance sheet in a way a large reactor cannot: the developer's model is a fleet of identical, standardised, factory-produced 0.45-0.5 MW blocks replicated across hundreds of sites, financed on the developer's balance sheet and amortised over a subscription. A modular reactor is the same product shape one or two orders of magnitude up in unit size. Relocatability also matches the RaaS covenant that the developer takes the asset away at end of term rather than leaving a stranded plant on the host's land.

State third-party retail-sale restrictions in regulated states (the reason today's providers sell availability, not kWh)
A reactor idle for 8,700 hours a year has no revenue; the RaaS subsidy comes from merchant grid-services participation a reactor cannot replicate
Emergency planning zone and security force obligations attach to the host's site, not the developer's

records.nuclear_fit: Excluded by construction, and the exclusion has now been tested. Adopted 25.513(b)(3)(A)(vi) requires a package to 'provide power sourced from a combination of natural gas or propane with photovoltaic panels and battery storage,' and new subparagraph (vii) requires it to 'prioritize power sourced from natural gas when it is available on site.' records.nuclear_fit: The waiver text describes an HCMS as a small-scale grid fed by 'clean energy technologies like fuel cells, solar panels, wind turbines, and energy storage systems.' A reactor cannot start in 10 seconds and cannot be black-started on demand at all; if it is already running, it can carry the load through an outage, but then it is the NORMAL power source, not the emergency one, and the facility still owes a code-compliant emergency supply behind it. So the honest nuclear read on healthcare is: a reactor displaces the utility feed and the diesels' RUN HOURS, not the diesels themselves, unless the microgrid pairs it with a battery that provides the 10-second ride-through — which is exactly the Kaiser architecture with a reactor swapped in for the fuel cell.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW unit is the only reactor size that matches a medical campus's actual essential-electrical-system load (a large hospital's whole campus is single-digit MW). The Kaiser precedent shows the certified article is a 1 MW fuel cell plus a 9 MWh battery — a microreactor is a drop-in for that fuel cell block at the same order of magnitude, whereas a 300 MW reactor has no addressable customer of that shape.

Long-term care facilities providing life support are excluded from the waiver and must keep a generator
State AHJ still certifies independently (in California, HCAI) — the CMS waiver does not bind the state
The waiver is an election, not an approval, so the facility carries the risk if a surveyor disagrees

records.name: EPA RICE NESHAP emergency-engine hour cap (40 CFR 63.6640(f)) — the rule that keeps diesel a sunk cost, not an asset
records.what_it_is: Federal air rules give standby engines a cheap compliance path only if they stay 'emergency' engines. An emergency stationary reciprocating internal combustion engine may run at most 100 hours per calendar year for maintenance, testing and specified non-emergency purposes, of which at most 50 hours may be genuine non-emergency operation — and those 50 hours may not be used for peak shaving, non-emergency demand response, or to earn income by supplying power to a grid. There is no contract here: the rule is a boundary condition on every diesel-replacement business case, because it forbids the diesel fleet from ever earning its keep. The host therefore carries 100% of the capital, maintenance, fuel-turnover and permitting cost of an asset that is contractually barred from producing revenue.

records.term: perpetual condition of the air permit
records.price_form: not a price — a use restriction that strands the host's capital

precedents.parties: Virginia DEQ (Mike Dowd, Air and Renewable Energy Division) <-> data-centre operators; opposed by Southern Environmental Law Center and Piedmont Environmental Council
precedents.size: ~9,000 permitted generators in Virginia, ~4,700 of them in Loudoun County; ~8,000 are Tier II
precedents.note: DEQ's 30 September 2025 memo would widen what counts as an 'emergency' to include utility 'planned outage' events noticed within 14 days, which is precisely the class of hours the federal emergency-engine definition excludes. The scale of the fight is the tell: the hour cap is the binding constraint on whether a very large installed diesel fleet is usable for anything.

records.nuclear_fit: A reactor is not a RICE engine and is not hour-capped by this rule at all — it can run 8,760 hours a year and sell into the grid, which is the exact freedom the diesel fleet is denied. That inverts the business case: diesel is a pure cost centre that can never amortise, while a reactor's capital can be amortised against continuous output. But the same inversion is the trap: a reactor sized to cover an emergency load will be economically dead unless it can sell its output the other 99% of the time, which throws it back onto the interconnection and third-party-sale questions the diesel fleet never has to answer.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW unit is small enough to be sized to a site's actual continuous load rather than its peak emergency load, so it can plausibly run at high capacity factor behind the meter and never need to export — sidestepping both the hour cap and the export/third-party-sale problem in one move. A 300 MW+ unit at a single host cannot do that.
blockers: The 100-hour cap makes diesel cheap-per-year to keep, which raises the bar an alternative must clear on total cost, not on emissions
Air permits are issued per engine by the state/local authority, so the replacement conversation is 50 different regulators, not one
Nothing in the RICE rule says what may legally replace a diesel engine as the emergency supply — that is a fire-code question (see NFPA/CMS records)

records.name: California Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP) — a ratepayer-funded capital subsidy with a closed technology list, an efficiency gate, and an explicit ban on backup-only assets
records.what_it_is: CPUC-administered, ratepayer-funded capital incentives paid to a Host Customer (or assigned to the developer) for behind-the-meter storage and generation. The applicant reserves an incentive, builds, and is paid on commissioning and, for storage, on performance. For a diesel-replacement question this programme is the most instructive rulebook in the country because its exclusions are explicit: equipment 'capable of operating on, or switching to, diesel fuel or diesel cycle for start-up or continuous operation' is ineligible, and so — critically — are 'backup systems intended solely for emergency purposes'. Generation must also clear a minimum operating efficiency gate: either waste-heat utilisation of at least 5% under P.U. Code 216.6(a), or electrical efficiency of at least 40%.

records.nuclear_fit: Three independent disqualifications, each of which would need a CPUC rulemaking to change. (1) Nuclear is absent from the closed eligible-technology list — not banned, just not enumerated, which in a programme with an enumerated list is the same thing. (2) The minimum operating efficiency gate requires 40% electrical efficiency OR meaningful waste-heat utilisation; a light-water microreactor operating electricity-only sits around 30-33% thermal-to-electric and would FAIL, so the only compliant configuration is CHP with a real thermal host. (3) The sizing rule caps incentivised capacity at the Host Customer's own annual peak demand and requires combined on-site generation to be no more than the host's maximum site electric load — the same output-cap trap as the third-party-sale rules.

The sizing cap at the host's own peak demand is again only satisfiable at 1-20 MW.

40% electrical efficiency / waste-heat utilisation gate that an electricity-only light-water microreactor fails
'Backup systems intended solely for emergency purposes' are explicitly ineligible — the programme will not pay for resilience alone
Incentivised capacity capped at the Host Customer's previous 12-month annual peak demand
System must be installed on the Host Customer's side of the utility meter and interconnected to the distribution system

records.name: Federal Energy Savings Performance Contract (ESPC) task order — how a federal site buys resilience with zero appropriated capex
records.what_it_is: A federal agency issues a task order under an ESPC IDIQ to an energy service company (ESCO). The ESCO designs, finances, builds, owns during the term, and operates the energy assets; the government pays nothing up front and instead pays the ESCO out of the utility and O&M savings the project generates, with those savings contractually guaranteed by the ESCO and measured and verified annually. If the savings do not materialise, the ESCO makes up the shortfall. Resilience assets (microgrid controls, on-site generation, storage) ride along inside a package whose repayment is carried by the efficiency measures. This is the mechanism by which a base gets a microgrid without ever asking Congress for military construction money.

records.term: up to 25 years by statute; Parris Island is 22 years
records.asset_owner: third-party developer (ESCO owns and operates through the performance period; title typically transfers at the end)
records.price_form: no capex — the government pays an annual payment funded entirely from contractually guaranteed utility and O&M savings

precedents.name: Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island microgrid
precedents.parties: Naval Facilities Engineering and Expeditionary Warfare Center (NAVFAC EXWC) <-> Ameresco
precedents.size: 3.5 MW gas CHP + 6.7 MW-DC solar PV + 8.0 MWh battery, with fast load-shedding microgrid control across 121 buildings

records.nuclear_fit: ESPC is structurally hostile to nuclear for one specific reason: the payment stream is capped by verified energy and O&M SAVINGS relative to the baseline utility bill, and it must repay the full project cost within 25 years. A reactor's capital cost per kW is far above what a federal site's utility savings can amortise, so the arithmetic fails before any licensing question arises. The related UESC (Utility Energy Service Contract) vehicle is more promising because the serving utility finances the work and there is no statutory savings-repayment test of the same severity. Separately, DoD has been buying nuclear outside these vehicles — via direct power purchase and pilot authorities — precisely because ESPC cannot carry it.
records.microreactor_edge: Real but narrow: at a genuinely remote or islanded federal site, the displaced baseline is not grid power at $0.08/kWh but delivered diesel, and delivered-diesel costs at remote sites are high enough that an ESPC savings stream could plausibly amortise a small unit. The fuel-logistics tail is the savings line item — a microreactor with a multi-year refuelling interval removes the convoy, the fuel farm and the fuel-quality maintenance, all of which are O&M savings an ESCO is allowed to count.
blockers: Statutory 25-year maximum term and the requirement that guaranteed savings repay the entire project cost
Annual measurement and verification of savings — a reactor's output is easy to verify but its cost is not repayable from savings at typical grid baselines
ESCO owns the asset during the term; an ESCO becoming an NRC licensee is unprecedented
Federal site nuclear siting adds NEPA and NRC review on a timeline no ESPC task order schedule contemplates

records.what_it_is: Where a PPA would make the developer an illegal retail supplier, the same economics can be papered as a true lease: the third party keeps title to the equipment but hands the host possession and use of it, with few restrictions on how the host uses it. The host is then generating its own power with rented equipment, and the owner is not selling electricity at all. Whether this works turns entirely on the lease terms — a lease that reserves operational control to the owner is a disguised PPA and fails.

NRC licensing assumes an operating organisation; splitting title from operation needs deliberate structuring

precedents.parties: N.C. Clean Energy Technology Center (DSIRE), tracking all 50 states
precedents.size: At least 29 states plus Washington DC and Puerto Rico authorize or allow third-party PPAs for solar PV

records.nuclear_fit: The size caps are the finding that matters and nobody writes them down in a nuclear context. In Texas, Colorado and Nevada the authorisation to sell behind the meter is conditioned on the system generating no more than roughly the host's own annual consumption (100%, 120%, 150% respectively). A reactor sized only to a single host's load has no scale economics, and a reactor sized to serve several hosts or export is outside the authorisation and becomes a regulated utility. In North Carolina and South Carolina a third-party sale is flatly prohibited, so a reactor developer must lease the machine to the host and let the host be the operator — which collides directly with NRC licensing, since the host would then need to be the licensee. The commercial structure and the licensing structure are coupled through this rule and neither can be chosen independently.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW unit is the only reactor scale that can sit under a 100-150% of-host-consumption cap at a real industrial or campus load without wasting most of its output. records.name: Tariffed on-bill lease of a customer-sited backup asset, paid for by aggregating it into a virtual power plant
records.what_it_is: The regulated utility leases a backup asset to the customer under a commission-approved tariff and bills it monthly on the electric bill. The customer gets seamless backup power; the utility gets dispatch rights over the asset during system peaks and aggregates thousands of them into a virtual power plant, and the peak-shaving value is what holds the lease price below the customer's cost of buying the same hardware. A parallel 'bring your own device' track pays a rebate to customers who buy their own asset and enrol it for shared dispatch. This is the cleanest example of the general principle that a backup asset only becomes affordable when someone is allowed to USE it between emergencies — the exact freedom the RICE NESHAP denies a diesel engine.

records.nuclear_fit: The mechanism does not scale to a reactor at a single host, but its economic logic is the one a reactor most needs and most easily satisfies: the asset earns its keep between emergencies. A reactor's problem is the mirror image of a battery's — the battery has near-zero marginal cost and limited energy, the reactor has large capital and unlimited energy — so the tariffed-lease structure would have to invert: the utility leases the reactor's OUTPUT to the host continuously and the host's resilience is a by-product, rather than leasing a standby asset and monetising it occasionally. The regulatory precedent that matters is narrower and more useful: a state commission has already approved putting a customer-sited generation asset on the utility's tariff and billing it on-bill, which is a shape a commission could in principle extend.
records.microreactor_edge: The VPM/aggregation logic argues for a fleet of small units across many hosts rather than one large unit at one host: 4,800 devices at 2,900 customers aggregate into 50 MW. A fleet of 5 MW units across ten critical facilities on one utility's system is the same portfolio shape and gives the utility a dispatchable resource with diversity, which one 50 MW machine does not.

Utility ownership of customer-sited generation is contested or barred outside vertically integrated states
A leased reactor makes the lessee-or-lessor question an NRC licensing question, not a commercial one

records.nuclear_fit: This is the cleanest example of a technology list excluding nuclear by construction rather than by hostility. Three separate clauses each independently disqualify a reactor: (1) the package must be a combination of generator + PV + batteries + on-site fuel, and 'on-site fuel' in the rule's sense is natural gas or propane; (2) the whole package must be under 2.5 MW, which is below even the small end of most microreactor designs and far below the point where reactor economics work; (3) the package must be 'stand-alone' and behind-the-meter with no export under any circumstance, which forecloses the capacity-factor economics a reactor needs. Getting nuclear into a programme like this requires the statute or rule to be amended, not a waiver.

records.name: Uptime Institute Tier III/IV engine-generator rating rule — the private standard that requires the diesel fleet to exist and to be unlimited-runtime
records.what_it_is: Not a law and not a contract, but the certification that data-centre tenants, lenders and insurers actually ask for. Uptime Institute's Tier Standard requires that the on-site engine generators for a Tier III or Tier IV site carry a rating with NO limitation on consecutive hours of operation at N demand: only continuous ratings, derated prime ratings, or standby ratings without runtime limits qualify. Tier I and Tier II may use runtime-limited machines. The practical effect is that the highest-value data-centre sites are contractually and commercially obliged to keep a fleet of engine generators capable of running indefinitely — which is why the diesel fleet survives even at sites that have added batteries, fuel cells or on-site gas.
records.who_signs: Uptime Institute <-> the owner/operator seeking Tier Certification; downstream this appears as a covenant in colocation contracts, tenant SLAs and lender/insurer diligence
records.term: per-certification; re-verified on Tier Certification of Constructed Facility and operational sustainability reviews
records.price_form: not priced — a design constraint that mandates capital the host cannot avoid

precedents.name: Uptime Institute Accredited Tier Designer Technical Paper: Engine-Generator Ratings
precedents.parties: Uptime Institute (standards body) <-> Tier-certified data centre operators worldwide
precedents.size: applies to every Tier III and Tier IV certified facility
precedents.note: Document reference UITPEGEN211-2026. The rule creates a direct collision with EPA RICE NESHAP: the federal rule gives an engine cheap 'emergency' status only if it runs under 100 hours a year, while Uptime requires the machine's RATING to have no runtime limit at all. Operators satisfy both by buying continuous-rated iron and then never using it — the worst possible capital outcome, and the strongest economic argument for replacing it with something that can run.

records.nuclear_fit: A reactor is the only candidate replacement that trivially satisfies the 'no limitation on consecutive hours of operation' requirement — it is the unlimited-runtime machine par excellence. But the Tier Standard is written around engine generators as the ENGINE-GENERATOR component of a topology, and the standard's other requirements (N+1 redundancy of the engine-generator system, concurrent maintainability, fault tolerance) mean a single reactor cannot by itself be the Tier III/IV backup: it would need redundant units or a paired conventional fleet. Uptime has no published pathway that treats a reactor as the engine-generator component.
records.microreactor_edge: The N+1 and concurrent-maintainability requirements reward small identical units over one large one. A Tier IV topology needs the engine-generator system to be fault-tolerant and maintainable while carrying load, which is impossible with one 300 MW reactor and arithmetically straightforward with a fleet of 5-10 MW factory-built units that can be individually taken offline. This is the clearest case in this dataset where the STANDARD, not the economics, prefers small and modular.
blockers: Uptime Tier Standard names engine generators as the engine-generator component; no published nuclear pathway
N+1 redundancy and concurrent maintainability mean one reactor is never sufficient on its own
Tier III/IV certification is bought by tenants and lenders, so the operator cannot unilaterally deviate
Direct conflict with the RICE NESHAP 100-hour cap means the incumbent fleet is already over-specified and under-used, which sets a high bar for a replacement's utilisation story

records.nuclear_fit: Excluded three separate ways, any one of which is fatal. (1) The eligible-equipment list is a closed enumeration — storage plus eleven named generation technologies (pressure reduction turbines, PV, wind, gas turbines, waste heat to power, microturbines, steam turbine CHP, internal combustion engines, linear generators, fuel cell CHP, fuel cell electric) — with no performance-based route in. (2) The generation budget is a *renewable* generation budget: 'Eligible fuels are those that produce useful energy when undergoing combustion or a chemical reaction and are classified as renewable', and customers 'are required to use 100% renewable fuel for the lifetime of the project'. Fission is neither combustion nor a chemical reaction, and is not renewable in California law. (3) The 40% electrical-efficiency gate is written as E/F_HHV, a ratio of rated electric output to *higher heating value fuel consumption* — a quantity that is undefined for a reactor, so the qualifying test cannot even be evaluated, let alone passed. Separately, the ineligibility of 'Backup systems intended solely for emergency purposes' is confirmed verbatim, and it cuts against diesel gensets as well: an emergency-only genset cannot claim SGIP either.
records.microreactor_edge: SGIP is the clearest place a *relocatable* microreactor is worse off than a fixed one. The handbook's permanence test says only systems permanently installed 'both physically and contractually' are eligible, and it names the disqualifiers: 'unsecured equipment, wheels, carrying handles, dolly, trailer, or platform, will deem the system ineligible'. Factory-built, truck-delivered, take-it-back-at-end-of-life is the microreactor's whole product story and it is the exact fact pattern this clause rejects. The 60-day written notice required before any change of site location or system ownership within the warranty period compounds it. The 3 MW incentive ceiling also caps the subsidy at the very bottom of the 1-20 MW band.

records.name: All-source RFP guarantee stack — what a utility makes the pair contractually promise
records.what_it_is: Utilities now run technology-neutral all-source RFPs and publish the contract they intend to sign, so a bidder's obligations are known before the bid. For storage the published template is not a price sheet, it is a stack of tested guarantees: a Guaranteed Storage Power Capacity Rating, a Guaranteed Storage Round Trip Efficiency, a Storage Availability Guarantee, a Storage Ramp Rate test, energy capacity tests, cybersecurity requirements, and a licensed professional engineer's certification of each at commercial operation. The utility also supplies and owns the Charging Energy and issues Charging and Discharging Notices to an AGC set-point, so the seller has no discretion over dispatch. Tax credits stay with the seller and are explicitly carved out of the capacity rights the utility buys.
records.who_signs: Bidder/project SPV <-> utility, on the utility's published RFP contract form, under state commission oversight
records.term: Set per RFP; the template's milestones, delay damages and security run from execution to commercial operation and through the delivery term
records.price_form: $/kW-month or $/kW-yr storage price (Exhibit K), adjusted by measured availability and round-trip efficiency

records.nuclear_fit: This is the concrete answer to 'what would a utility make a reactor promise'. Every line of the storage guarantee stack has a nuclear analogue and each is harder: guaranteed power capacity becomes guaranteed net electrical output at reference conditions; round-trip efficiency becomes thermal efficiency and house load; the availability guarantee becomes a capacity-factor guarantee net of refuelling; the ramp-rate test becomes the reactor's licensed manoeuvring envelope, which for most microreactor designs is the binding constraint. The professional-engineer certification at commercial operation is the interesting enabler: it means the utility's acceptance test is an engineering document, not a regulatory one, so a design that can demonstrate its numbers can be accepted on the same terms as a battery. The blocker is AGC: these templates give the utility direct set-point control of the asset, and no reactor licence contemplates a utility dispatcher moving reactor power.
records.microreactor_edge: Pairing solves the ramp-rate exhibit outright. A reactor cannot pass a storage ramp-rate test and should not try; a battery on the same point of delivery can, and the combined facility is what gets certified. That is the single most useful thing pairing does for a bid into an all-source RFP: it lets a slow, always-on machine be sold under a contract form written for fast machines. The relocatability of a 1-20 MW unit also changes the delay-damages and security calculus, since a factory unit that misses a milestone at one site is not a stranded construction project.
blockers: AGC set-point control by the utility is incompatible with current reactor licensing bases
Availability guarantees have to be quoted before any operating fleet exists to price them
Delay damages and milestone security in these templates assume construction schedules measured in quarters, not the multi-year NRC licensing tail

Capacity Rights carve-outs mean the seller keeps the tax credits — the utility will price the bid assuming those credits are monetised, which requires a tax-equity market that does not yet exist for microreactors

records.name: CMS categorical waiver for Health Care Microgrid Systems (QSO-23-11-LSC)
records.what_it_is: CMS conditions of participation bind hospitals to the 2012 edition of NFPA 99, which requires the emergency power source for a hospital's essential electric system to be a generator set or a battery system — nothing else. On 2023-03-31 CMS issued a categorical waiver letting facilities instead comply with the 2021 edition of NFPA 99 and the 2023 NEC, which permit a 'health care microgrid system' (HCMS) to be that source. Nobody signs anything: the facility formally elects the waiver, documents the election, and produces it at the survey entrance conference along with evidence of compliance. The economic consequence is that the capital otherwise sunk in a legally-mandated diesel plant becomes available to buy a different power source.

records.nuclear_fit: This is the single most consequential open door found in this pass, and it is open to reactors by the text of the standard, not by analogy. The CMS attachment reproduces NFPA 99 (2021) 6.10.2 as: any combination of generation, storage or transformation equipment may serve as the power source for all or a portion of an HCMS. The standard does not enumerate permitted generation technologies. A reactor plus a battery, behind an HCMS control system, is therefore already a permissible emergency power source for a CMS-certified hospital — with no CMS rulemaking required. The gating requirements are engineering, not nuclear: a control system isolated from other networks with its own 90-minute backup battery and a per-source power readout, a written commissioning plan and report, recommissioning every 5 years, and annual inspection/testing/maintenance by qualified persons.
records.microreactor_edge: The battery is what makes the reactor legally usable here. NFPA 110 Type 10 requires the emergency source to pick up load within 10 seconds; a reactor cannot start from cold in 10 seconds and should not be asked to try. A battery sized for minutes covers the transfer, the reactor carries the multi-day outage that the batteries at Ontario (10 hours) and Richmond (3 hours) cannot, and the pair covers both ends of the duration curve that neither covers alone. A 1-20 MW unit also matches the load: Ontario's whole hospital emergency need is covered by 9 MWh, so a single 5 MW block plus a small battery serves an entire medical campus with margin, and the same campus is exactly the 'individual buildings or campuses consisting of several buildings, and non-health care buildings' scope NFPA 99 6.10.1.3/6.10.1.4 permits an HCMS to serve.

State hospital building authorities are a second gate: in California HCAI/OSHPD reviews hospital electrical systems independently of CMS

records.name: ELCC capacity accreditation — what the pair is allowed to count as
records.what_it_is: In an organised capacity market the revenue a resource earns is its installed capacity multiplied by an accreditation factor set by the RTO, not by the owner. PJM computes an ELCC class rating for every class by adding an increment of that class to a probabilistic model and measuring how much expected unserved energy it removes, divided by what perfect capacity would remove. Nobody signs anything; the number is published annually and it moves. It is the single largest determinant of whether a paired asset earns capacity revenue, and it is where a steady generator and a duration-limited battery are valued on completely different curves.

records.nuclear_fit: Nuclear is accredited at 95% in PJM for 2027/2028 — the highest class rating of any generation class, above coal (83%), gas combined cycle (74%) and gas combustion turbine (61%). That is the strongest quantitative statement of nuclear's grid value found in this pass, and it is written into an RTO study rather than a vendor deck. The specific enabler for a pair is that accreditation is computed per class on a marginal, probabilistic basis: a resource that is available in the hours the model is short earns near-perfect credit, and a reactor's flat output plus a battery that shifts it into those hours is exactly that resource. The blocker is definitional: there is no ELCC class for a nuclear-storage hybrid, and PJM cannot even rate the solar-storage hybrid class for lack of sample.
records.microreactor_edge: The accreditation table is a pricing sheet for how much battery to buy. Going from 4-hr to 10-hr storage buys 20 accreditation points (58% -> 78%) and costs roughly 2.5x the energy capacity. Pairing a 5 MW always-on block with a 4-hour battery instead does something no amount of battery duration achieves: it removes the duration limit entirely, because the reactor refills the battery every night for free. A 1-20 MW unit is also small enough to be accredited behind the meter as load reduction rather than as generation — the Demand Resource class jumped to 92% for 2027/2028 after PJM eliminated the DR performance window and made DR a 24/7 resource, which is precisely the shape a reactor-plus-battery presents to the utility.

PJM lists Solar-Storage Hybrid as 'Small Sample Size' for both 2026/27 and 2027/28 — the hybrid precedent that would carry a reactor pair does not yet exist statistically
Class ratings are recomputed annually and moved by 8-9 points in one year for storage classes; a 20-year financing cannot be underwritten on them
Behind-the-meter assets at a single host are outside the capacity market entirely unless the utility tariff admits them

records.nuclear_fit: The ESA/P3 form is the natural wrapper for a reactor because it keeps the licensee and the operator in one entity — the developer — and gives the host a service it can procure without a nuclear engineering staff or a capital vote. Two things break. First, term: a microgrid ESA runs 15-25 years against a reactor's design life and licence renewal cycle, so the residual-value and decommissioning questions land inside the contract rather than after it. Second, the security and emergency-planning obligations of a licensed facility do not sit comfortably on a county correctional facility or a hospital campus, and no ESA template addresses them.
records.microreactor_edge: Montgomery County's two microgrids together deliver about 11 GWh/year, which is roughly 1.25 MW average. A single 5 MW block would serve that county's whole critical-facility portfolio four times over with the surplus available for export or heat — meaning the natural microreactor customer here is not one facility but an aggregated municipal or campus portfolio. Factory build and relocatability also match the P3 risk allocation: the developer's downside on a stranded asset is bounded if the unit can be removed and redeployed, which is not true of a CHP plant poured into a jail's mechanical yard.

records.nuclear_fit: The program's own selection criteria — independent operation for extended periods, multiple customers, critical facilities — describe a reactor better than they describe a solar-plus-battery microgrid, which is the awkward part. A $15 million cap is real money against a microreactor's cost but well short of it, so the mechanism as written can fund the storage and controls half of a reactor pairing but not the reactor. The harder blocker is political rather than financial: these programs are aimed at disadvantaged and tribal communities, and siting a first-of-a-kind licensed nuclear facility in exactly those communities is an environmental-justice problem that a grant application does not resolve.
records.microreactor_edge: Isla Vista is the sharpest number here: $15.3 million buys a community 24 hours of backup. A 1-20 MW unit's proposition against that is duration measured in years rather than hours, for a portfolio of sites rather than one — and the honest comparison is that the grant program has already spent its $200 million and is closed, so the mechanism cannot be the funding route for a reactor even if the fit were perfect. The useful read is the price signal, not the funding: California's regulator was willing to spend roughly $100,000 per critical-facility-day of resilience, which is the number a reactor-plus-storage resilience offering can be benchmarked against.

Award terms bind operation and maintenance for a minimum period without providing an operating revenue stream

records.name: Single-owner merchant pair — one entity owns generator and storage and optimises dispatch against price
records.what_it_is: No offtake contract at all: one owner holds both the generator and the battery, and the battery's job is to move the generator's flat output into the hours the market pays for. Because both halves are inside one balance sheet the owner is indifferent to which asset earns the revenue, and the optimisation is purely dispatch against a price series. The economics live or die on price volatility rather than on price level, which makes this the one mechanism where a market with cheap average power can still be the best market. It is also the mechanism most exposed: nothing is contracted, so nothing is bankable.
records.who_signs: Nobody — the owner sells into the wholesale market as a price taker; the counterparty is the market operator
records.term: Asset life; 20-year project life is the standard modelling assumption
records.price_form: merchant real-time market revenue, plus tax credits on the generation half

records.nuclear_fit: Idaho National Laboratory modelled exactly this structure for a reactor: a 20 MWth (9.6 MWe) high-temperature gas reactor with a single owner also holding a liquid metal battery, dispatched by stochastic optimisation against ERCOT, PJM and MISO real-time prices over a 20-year life. Two findings matter commercially. First, the battery prefers to charge from the reactor rather than from the grid, so the tax-credit charging restriction that constrains solar hybrids is close to free for a reactor pair. Second, the reactor's own capex dominates: INL's base case assumes $14,001/kWe with a low case of $8,616/kWe, and even at the low case the NPV outcome varies by market rather than being uniformly positive. The paper reports the maximum allowable reactor capex to break even, computed per 9,800 kW of reactor — which is the correct way to state the target and is rarely stated that way in vendor material.
records.microreactor_edge: The most surprising number in the literature is the sizing ratio. INL optimised the battery's power rating across a 0-100 MWe range against a 9.6 MWe reactor, and the optimum sat at the top of the range in all three markets — roughly ten times the reactor's electrical output, with the paper cautioning that beyond 100 MWe the estimates could differ. That is the opposite of the intuition that a small reactor takes a small battery: a flat generator plus a very large short-duration battery is a peaking plant with nuclear fuel. The other quantified finding is that a large share of the reactor's output is better sold as heat or product than as electricity — INL estimates non-electric application potential at 38.6% in ERCOT, 23.7% in PJM and 24% in MISO, and in ERCOT 650 MWh of 1,682 MWh generated is diverted to charging rather than sold. To make the arbitrage return real the battery must sustain 624-633 cycles per year at 72.2% round-trip efficiency, or 730-768 cycles at 80.3%.
blockers: Merchant revenue is unbankable for a first-of-a-kind asset; lenders will require an offtake contract that this mechanism by definition lacks
The measured arbitrage margin on a real utility contract was ~9% of cost — a difference between two large, volatile numbers
INL's own result is market-dependent: even at the low capex case the NPV varies significantly across ERCOT, PJM and MISO
624-768 full cycles per year is a duty cycle no commercially available long-life battery chemistry is warranted for over a 20-year life

records.name: Tax-credit charging restrictions — the rule that wrote the pairing into the contract
records.what_it_is: Before standalone storage became creditable, a battery only earned the investment credit by being part of a qualifying generator's property, and it only stayed creditable if it charged from that generator. The rule is a cliff plus a haircut measured annually over the five-year recapture period: below 75% of annual charging energy from the qualifying source the credit is lost entirely, and between 75% and 100% it is pro-rated. Nobody signs this either — it is tax law — but it is the reason hybrid PPAs and hybrid interconnection agreements contain explicit no-grid-charging covenants, metering obligations and control logic, and why those covenants persist as boilerplate. The IRS ruling that made it concrete describes charging control implemented in software sampling every 0.1 seconds.

records.term: Five-year recapture period, tested each annual measuring period

records.nuclear_fit: Nuclear is inside the technology-neutral credits: 48E and 45Y apply to zero-carbon generation regardless of technology, so a reactor and a battery can each claim on their own terms and the historical reason to bolt them together is gone. That is an enabler with a sting. The specific choice a reactor project faces, as INL frames it, is ITC versus PTC: high-capex, high-capacity-factor assets sit awkwardly between the two rules of thumb, since high capex argues for the ITC and high capacity factor argues for the PTC. At a $27/MWh PTC, INL finds the claimable PTC exceeds the microreactor's entire variable O&M cost.
records.microreactor_edge: For a 1-20 MW unit the ITC/PTC choice is closer than for a gigawatt plant because the capex per kW is much higher (INL models $14,001/kWe base and $8,616/kWe low case against a conventional plant's few thousand), which pushes toward the ITC, while a microreactor's design capacity factor pushes toward the PTC. The battery half matters here: INL explicitly excludes the LMB from the tax-credit modelling, noting this understates the pair's economics, so a real project can stack a 48E claim on the storage that the published analysis does not credit.

Recapture is tested annually for five years — an operating year in which the reactor is down for refuelling and the battery charges from the grid is a tax event, not just a performance event
Tax-equity covenants outlive the tax rule that created them; no-grid-charging language is still standard hybrid-PPA boilerplate
Credit rates depend on wage/apprenticeship, domestic content and energy-community tests that a relocatable factory-built unit may satisfy in one location and not another

records.name: Generator hybridisation — a small battery bolted onto a thermal unit to sell its start time
records.what_it_is: A short-duration battery is integrated into an existing thermal generator's controls so that the combined plant is dispatchable the instant the market calls it, while the turbine is still starting or entirely offline. The battery is not a storage product; it is a performance upgrade to the generator, and the two are bid into the market as one resource. It is bought because the *service* being sold is response time, and response time is where a thermal machine loses. Crucially the battery is tiny relative to the generator — the point is bridging seconds and minutes, not shifting hours.
records.who_signs: Plant owner (utility or IPP) <-> equipment vendor / integrator; the combined plant then bids under existing market rules
records.term: Plant life; the market products are bid daily
records.price_form: monetised through ancillary-service and energy market revenues, plus avoided fuel and emissions during starts

precedents.parties: Marin Clean Energy <-> existing 48 MW gas-fired peaker, Fresno, California

precedents.note: EIA counted at least 13 fossil-plus-storage hybrid plants operating between 2019 and 2022, down to 8 as of 2023 — the population is small and shrinking, which is itself a caution about this mechanism's durability.

records.nuclear_fit: Of every mechanism in this file, this is the closest structural match to a reactor, because it treats the battery as a control-system component rather than an energy asset. A reactor has the same defect as a peaker in an exaggerated form — it cannot follow a step change in load, and unlike a turbine it should not be asked to cycle at all, since thermal cycling is a licensing and materials problem rather than a fuel-cost one. The battery buys the reactor the right to run flat. What changes versus a gas turbine is the ratio: SCE needed 26 minutes of storage on a machine that starts in ten; a reactor is far slower to change power, so the buffer has to cover a longer transient.
records.microreactor_edge: SCE's ratio is the number worth carrying: 10 MW of battery power on a 50 MW turbine, at 4.3 MWh. Scaled to a 5 MW reactor that is roughly a 1 MW / 0.4 MWh buffer — small enough to sit in a couple of cabinets and to be replaced on a normal commercial cycle without touching the nuclear island. The reactor also gets something the peaker does not: because it runs continuously, the battery is always charged and always available, so the pair can offer instantaneous response without the peaker's dependence on a market signal to refill. Sizing the reactor to average load and letting the buffer absorb peaks is the specific move a 1-20 MW factory-built block enables, and it is what turns a flat 5 MW into a service.

Integrating a battery into a nuclear plant's control system crosses into safety-related design review in a way that bolting one onto a gas turbine does not
Market rules for co-located hybrids differ by ISO and mostly assume an intermittent host resource
The revenue is ancillary-service revenue, which is thin, saturates quickly, and is unavailable behind the meter

records.name: Grid-services contract — black start, synthetic inertia and fast frequency response bought as named products
records.what_it_is: Rather than buying energy or capacity, the utility contracts for named reliability services and specifies the physics: response time, inertia constant, MW of fast frequency response, and the ability to restart the grid from a blackout. The asset owner builds to those specifications and is paid a contracted fee; the utility gets services that were previously an unpriced by-product of having synchronous machines on the system. This is the mechanism by which a resource with no fuel and no synchronous mass gets paid for what a spinning turbine used to give away, and it is the newest of the mechanisms here.

records.nuclear_fit: Black start is the service a nuclear plant conspicuously cannot provide and conspicuously needs: large reactors are the classic black-start *load*, requiring an external cranking path to restore station power. A microreactor paired with a battery inverts that relationship at site scale — the battery is the grid-forming source, and the reactor is what the battery restarts. The commercial enabler is that these services are now separately contracted and separately paid, so a site pair can be compensated for a capability it must build anyway. The blocker is that grid-forming credit attaches to the inverter, not the generator, so the reactor half earns nothing under these products directly.
records.microreactor_edge: The 50 MW / 25 MWh fast-frequency-response block inside Kapolei is a 30-minute battery — the service is priced on power, not energy. That is exactly the shape a reactor pair needs: a 5 MW reactor with a 5 MW / 2.5 MWh grid-forming battery costs a fraction of a 4-hour system and buys the same sub-second response class. And a 1-20 MW unit's genuine differentiator is that after black start it can keep an islanded network alive indefinitely, whereas a battery-only black start on a dead grid runs out of energy in hours unless generation comes back.

Black start award prices are confidential in ERCOT's public market notices, so the revenue is real but not publicly benchmarkable
Grid-forming capability is an inverter attribute; a synchronous reactor plant earns the inertia credit but not the sub-second products
No nuclear resource has been contracted for black start service at any scale

records.name: Intentional islanding — the microgrid interconnect device certification gate
records.what_it_is: To island a site and re-synchronise, the customer must satisfy the utility that the on-site resources cannot back-feed a de-energised distribution circuit and that they transition safely between islanded and grid-parallel modes. In practice this is enforced through the interconnection application: the utility requires listed equipment certified to a named standard before it will approve the switch. The critical detail is that the standard everyone cites for DER interconnection, UL 1741 SB (implementing IEEE 1547-2018), does not test for this at all — so utilities have had to invent an additional requirement. Nobody is paid for anything here; it is a gate, and it is the gate every microgrid passes through.

records.term: Per interconnection agreement; permanent condition of operation
records.price_form: not priced — a certification and study cost borne by the applicant

precedents.size: Applies to all NY interconnection applications for DERs with microgrid interconnect devices (MIDs) and to EVs with V2G/V2H
precedents.note: February 2025. The JU found that New York's Standardized Interconnection Requirements do not check that DERs in an intentional island cannot back-feed a de-energised area EPS, and do not check safe transition between islanded and utility-interactive modes. UL 1741 SB, the SIR's baseline requirement, has no intentional-islanding type test, and its 'Enter Service' test does not apply to islanded systems. The JU therefore imposed a separate UL 1741 CRD for Multi-Mode Products requirement on top of IEEE 1547-2018 and UL 1741 SB.

precedents.note: Islands the hospital for roughly three hours, demonstrating that the practical constraint on an islanded medical campus is not the switchgear but the energy behind it.

records.nuclear_fit: Islanding is where a reactor's normal handicap inverts. Everything in IEEE 1547 / UL 1741 is written for inverter-based resources whose failure mode is back-feeding a dead line; a rotating-machine reactor plant behind a microgrid interconnect device sits on the older, better-understood side of that rulebook, closer to how a standby generator is treated than how a PV inverter is. The blocker is the reverse of the battery's: an inverter can form a grid in milliseconds and a reactor cannot, so the reactor cannot be the resource that catches the island at the instant of separation. It has to already be running, or the battery has to hold the island until it is.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW block plus a battery is the only combination that both catches the island and holds it. The battery's grid-forming inverter picks up the island inside the sub-second window the certification is about; the reactor then carries it for days, which no battery at hospital scale does — Richmond's 1 MWh gives three hours, Ontario's 9 MWh gives ten. The pair also collapses a sizing problem: without a reactor the battery must be sized to the worst-case outage duration, and with one it need only be sized to the transfer transient plus a ramp margin, which is one to two orders of magnitude less energy.

State interconnection rules are being amended one utility group at a time — a project designed to the published SIR can still be rejected on an added requirement
The certification path is written around inverters; a reactor's protection and synchronisation scheme has no listed-equipment shortcut and will be evaluated by study
Re-synchronisation to the area EPS after an island is the utility's call, not the host's

records.nuclear_fit: This is the mechanism most favourable to a reactor, because the benchmark is a transmission project rather than a commodity price. National Grid's alternative was a $200 million cable; that is roughly $33,000 per kW of the 6 MW it was firming, which is more than double INL's high-end microreactor capex assumption of $14,001/kWe. The blocker is regulatory rather than economic: rate-basing a reactor requires the utility to be the NRC licensee and to convince a state commission to put a first-of-a-kind nuclear asset in customer rates, which is exactly the argument that has historically gone badly. It also has to survive prudence review if the unit underperforms.
records.microreactor_edge: Nantucket is the archetypal microreactor site and the numbers say so: an island with a hard cable constraint, a summer peak, an existing diesel plant, and a utility willing to spend $81 million to avoid $200 million. A 5-15 MW reactor replaces both the 15 MW diesel and most of the 48 MWh battery, and unlike the battery it does not need the cable at all to recharge — the 8-hour battery's entire value depends on being refilled off-peak through the very cables it is insuring against. That dependency is the specific weakness a reactor removes, and it is invisible in the headline MW/MWh.
blockers: Rate-basing puts the utility on the NRC licence and the prudence risk; no US utility has done this for a microreactor

The comparison only works where the avoided wires cost is enormous; on an unconstrained system there is nothing to defer

records.name: Single hybrid PPA — generator and storage sold as one $/kWh product
records.what_it_is: One contract, one price, one point of delivery: the developer owns the generator and the battery as a single facility and sells a shaped, dispatchable energy product at a flat $/kWh. The offtaker does not see two assets and does not pay separately for storage — the battery is an input to the seller's delivery obligation, not a product. The seller therefore carries all of the pairing risk (round-trip losses, degradation, augmentation) inside a single energy price, and the buyer's only real levers are the delivery schedule and the availability/curtailment terms. This is the form utility RFPs now default to, and it is why the storage cost shows up as a per-MWh adder rather than a line item.

records.nuclear_fit: A single hybrid PPA is the closest existing template for selling a reactor-plus-storage block, because it sells the service rather than the machines — which is what a host actually wants and what keeps the reactor's operating envelope out of the contract. The blocker is that in a solar hybrid the battery exists to make an intermittent source firm; with a reactor the vector reverses. The reactor is already firm and the battery exists to make it *flexible* — to absorb the difference between a flat thermal output and a spiky site load. That flips who benefits from the charging terms: a solar hybrid's PPA restricts grid charging to protect the renewable attribute, whereas a reactor hybrid wants the battery charged almost exclusively from the reactor anyway, which makes the restriction free to accept.
records.microreactor_edge: The pricing benchmark transfers directly and it is brutal: Hawai'i, the highest-cost major US grid, buys firm-shaped renewable energy at 9 cents/kWh on a 25-year term. A 1-20 MW reactor selling into any grid-connected hybrid PPA has to clear that. Where the microreactor wins is where the hybrid PPA cannot go at all — off-grid, islanded, or behind a meter where the alternative is diesel at 30-70 cents/kWh, not solar at 9. The right read of this mechanism is that it sets the ceiling price for grid-tied reactor pairs and tells you to sell somewhere else.
blockers: A single blended $/kWh forces the seller to absorb degradation and augmentation risk over 25 years — for a battery that is an actuarial problem, for a reactor it is a refuelling and licence-renewal problem the counterparty has never priced
Legacy ITC charging restrictions shaped these contracts (see itc-charging-restriction record) and still appear as boilerplate in hybrid PPAs even where the tax rule no longer requires them
9 cents/kWh in Hawai'i is the number to beat; nothing in the current microreactor cost literature gets there on a grid-tied basis

records.nuclear_fit: The tolling form transfers cleanly to a reactor because it already separates ownership from dispatch: the vendor/SPV owns and operates the plant (which is what NRC licensing wants — a single, competent licensee), and the host or utility buys the right to call on it. What does not transfer is the price form. A battery is paid $/kW-month precisely because it has no fuel and no energy of its own; a reactor generates, so the analogue is a capacity-plus-energy split (a $/kW-month availability fee for the firm block, plus $/MWh for what it actually delivers). The guaranteed-efficiency schedule has a direct reactor analogue that no battery contract has: a guaranteed capacity-factor / availability schedule net of scheduled refuelling and maintenance outages, which is the one number a nuclear tolling agreement will be negotiated on.
records.microreactor_edge: A 300 MW/1,200 MWh toll is a wholesale-market instrument; a 1-20 MW reactor's version is the same paper at a site-sized scale, where the offtaker is a single host rather than a utility. The relevant arithmetic: Anaheim is paying $18.76/kW-month = ~$225/kW-yr for 4 hours of shiftable energy with zero energy of its own. A 5 MW reactor plus a 2-4 hour battery sold on the same $/kW-month basis has to clear that number and the diesel it displaces, but it also sells firm energy the battery cannot, so it competes on the energy leg, not the capacity leg.
blockers: Capacity payments are priced off a market's resource-adequacy value; a behind-the-meter reactor at a single host has no RA market to monetise unless the utility tariff lets it export
Tolling puts availability risk on the owner — a reactor owner cannot yet quote a bankable availability guarantee for a first-of-a-kind unit
$100/kW development and operation security is trivial for a battery developer and material for a reactor SPV with a decade-long licensing tail

records.nuclear_fit: Surplus interconnection is the strongest structural fit nuclear has in the whole interconnection landscape, and it is the mechanism behind the coal-to-nuclear thesis: a retiring thermal plant leaves behind a studied, energised, high-voltage POI sized for a firm baseload machine with a similar capacity factor - which is exactly the profile a reactor presents, and unlike solar it will actually use the headroom around the clock. records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW unit fits into headroom that is too small to interest anyone else. A retiring 300 MW coal unit's POI is a target for a large developer; the 5-15 MW of unused headroom at a small industrial cogen site, a retired peaker, or a partially-derated plant is not, and that is precisely the size a microreactor fills. Because MISO surplus projects have come online in about a year on average since 2024, a factory-built unit whose site works is schedule-compatible with the connection route for the first time. A relocatable fleet can also be pointed at wherever the headroom is, rather than needing the headroom to appear where the host already is.

records.nuclear_fit: Ignores nuclear — and that neutrality is the opening. Schedule DCT never enumerates generation technologies. Its 'Customer-Owned Generation and Emergency Conditions' section lets a customer elect to use behind-the-meter generation to offset its Contract Capacity, on one engineering condition: equipment must exist 'to instantaneously curtail load equal to or greater than the behind-the-meter generation output', plus an OAC 4901:1-22 interconnection agreement. Because the customer's exposure is a minimum billing demand rather than metered consumption, a BTM generator that merely shaves energy saves nothing — only lowering Contract Capacity itself does. That makes the netting election the single most valuable clause in the tariff for a reactor developer: every MW of firm on-site capacity that reduces Contract Capacity removes roughly 0.85 MW of minimum billing demand for the full 11-12 year term, and reduces the 50%-of-minimum-charges collateral in proportion. Emergency or backup generation not designed to run in parallel is expressly outside these requirements — the escape hatch a diesel farm uses and a baseload reactor cannot.
records.microreactor_edge: A 25 MW data centre is the smallest load Schedule DCT reaches, and it is served entirely by the top of the 1-20 MW microreactor band or a two-unit plant — so the microreactor is the only reactor class that can address the tariff's entry tier rather than only hyperscale campuses. The instantaneous-curtailment requirement is also easier to satisfy for a small, steadily-loaded unit than for a large one whose trip drops a step the site cannot absorb. Against that, the tariff's site rule ('must own or have the exclusive right to use the land') and the 8-year-post-ramp commitment are indifferent to relocatability, so the microreactor's mobility earns nothing here.

records.name: DOE cost-shared cooperative agreement: the government buys down half the first-of-a-kind capex and owns none of it
records.what_it_is: DOE signs a multi-year cooperative agreement with a developer under which the two sides split total project cost, invoice by invoice, against agreed technical milestones. DOE takes no ownership, no output and no equity; it buys the existence of a first unit. The Energy Policy Act of 2005 sets the default floor - a non-federal share of not less than 50% for demonstration and commercial application activities - and the ARDP funding opportunity applied that floor to every invoice in every year rather than averaging it over the award, which is a materially tighter constraint than a headline 50-50 implies. Because the split is on total project cost, DOE's dollar commitment is a ceiling, not a budget: it only pays out if the developer spends its half first.

records.nuclear_fit: A 50% cost share is the only instrument that has moved a first-of-a-kind reactor from paper to a construction site in the United States, and its structural weakness is exactly the thing it is praised for: because DOE pays a percentage of whatever the project costs, a cost overrun is shared rather than absorbed, so neither party has the incentive a fixed-price contract creates. It also does not solve the offtake problem at all - a fully cost-shared reactor still has no customer, which is what killed the one ARDP-adjacent project that had a price.
records.microreactor_edge: The 50% floor is written as a percentage, so it is technology-neutral and scale-neutral - which quietly disadvantages microreactors twice. First, at $2-4 billion of total project cost a large demonstration can absorb a nine-figure federal award, while a $50-150 million microreactor's 50% is a rounding error to DOE and does not justify the cooperative agreement's administrative load. Second, the developer must fund its half BEFORE invoicing, and for a microreactor firm that means raising the entire unit cost in venture equity anyway - which is why the microreactor cohort ended up in the DOE Reactor Pilot Program's no-money authorisation pathway instead of in ARDP.
blockers: DOE's dollar commitment is 'subject to the availability of future appropriations' - it is a ceiling, not a budget
The non-federal 50% applies to each invoice each year, so a developer that cannot fund its half stops drawing federal money immediately
Percentage cost share shares overruns rather than capping them; nobody holds fixed-price risk
Cost share does not create an offtaker - a fully cost-shared reactor still has no customer
Widely repeated siting facts from the 2021-22 award record are stale: the Xe-100 demonstration is in Texas, not Washington

Tariff I.P.'s Special Terms are explicit that a customer with its own generation buys standby service and must 'contract for the maximum amount of demand in kW which the Company might be required to furnish' — so behind-the-meter generation does not reduce the contracted demand, it defines it. Worse, the tariff's standing path for customer generation routes to 'Rider NMS (Net Metering Service Rider), Tariff COGEN/SPP or by special agreement with the Company' — and a fission plant is neither a cogeneration facility nor a PURPA small power production facility, whose fuel must be biomass, waste, renewable resources or geothermal. A reactor host in I&M territory therefore has exactly one route, the bilateral special agreement, with no tariffed terms to fall back on. This is the sharpest contrast in the file: Ohio lets BTM output offset Contract Capacity subject to instantaneous curtailment; Indiana makes BTM output irrelevant to the bill.

The 70 MW single-plant threshold is 2.8x AEP Ohio's 25 MW, so no single microreactor and no plausible small fleet reaches the tier at all — a 1-20 MW unit is invisible to this tariff except as the on-site generator of a customer who is already there for other reasons. The 150 MW affiliate-aggregation rule with a 1 MW per-premises floor also means a distributed fleet of small sites can be swept into Large Load status collectively while no individual site qualifies for anything.

records.name: Rate-regulated utility ownership: the reactor goes in the rate base, not into a PPA
records.what_it_is: A regulated utility - or a Crown corporation under an economic regulator - owns the reactor outright, capitalises it, and recovers construction cost plus an allowed return through regulated rates. There is no offtaker and no price per MWh negotiated with anyone: the counterparty is the entire captive customer base, and the 'contract' is a commission order setting payment amounts. This is the only structure in which a small reactor's full capital cost has ever been published, because rate regulation forces disclosure that a bilateral PPA does not. It is also the structure that puts 100% of construction-cost overrun risk on ratepayers unless the commission disallows it.

records.nuclear_fit: Rate-basing is the oldest way to finance a reactor and remains the only one that has actually produced a published all-in number for a small unit. What nuclear changes is who absorbs the overrun: in a PPA the developer eats it, in a rate base the customer does, which is why commissions resist and why the two North American small-reactor rate-base cases are both public or Crown entities (OPG, TVA) rather than investor-owned utilities. Note also that PacifiCorp's route to TerraPower's 345 MWe Natrium unit at Kemmerer is a power purchase agreement, not ownership - and PacifiCorp has not disclosed the price, so even the utility-adjacent case does not yield a number.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW unit is too small to matter to a rate base and too small to justify the proceeding. OPG's CAD 6.1 billion first unit is a project a regulator will spend two years examining; a CAD 60-100 million microreactor is below the threshold at which most commissions open a certificate proceeding at all, and its cost disappears inside a utility's ordinary capital budget. The consequence cuts both ways: the microreactor escapes the prudence review that OPG's unit must survive, and it also never generates the public cost disclosure that review produces - which is exactly why no microreactor capital cost is public and OPG's is.

records.name: Co-located load / behind-the-meter generation at a generating facility
records.what_it_is: The load moves to the generator rather than the generator moving to the load. A large customer sits inside the plant fence and takes power directly from the generator, netting some or all of its demand behind the meter, with the plant's existing interconnection agreement amended to describe the arrangement. Because the load is not a new transmission-connected load and the generator is not a new interconnection request, the arrangement can in principle skip both queues entirely - which is exactly why FERC has spent 2024-2026 fighting over whether it is lawful.

records.nuclear_fit: The single most important negative precedent in this space is nuclear. On 1 November 2024 FERC rejected, 2-1, the amended Susquehanna ISA that would have raised Amazon's co-located data centre load from 300 MW to 480 MW (with a path to 960 MW in 120 MW increments), on the ground that PJM had not justified the non-conforming provisions. That rejection is what triggered the EL25-49 show-cause proceeding. So the co-location route for a reactor is not a settled commercial structure - it is an open FERC docket in which the first mover was told no, and where the pending remedy explicitly includes a cap on how much load may be netted behind the meter.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW unit is small enough that the co-located load can plausibly be ALL of the plant's output, which is the cleanest version of this structure: no export, no netting question, no capacity-market interaction, and arguably no interconnection request at all. The FERC fight is about hundreds of megawatts being pulled out of a capacity market; a 5 MW machine serving a 5 MW hospital or fab does not create the resource-adequacy problem that made Susquehanna contentious. But watch the pending BTMG MW threshold - if PJM sets it low, it binds small units too, and if it is set high, the microreactor case is trivially inside it.

This is the fastest-moving area of US interconnection law in 2025-2026 and it is where any on-site reactor serving a large host will actually land.

records.nuclear_fit: A host powered by an on-site reactor is a strong candidate for the curtailable fast path precisely because it does not need the grid for energy - it needs the grid for backup. Agreeing to be curtailed costs a self-supplied host far less than it costs a grid-dependent one, which is a real and underused argument. The catch is ERCOT's version: SB6 makes curtailability mandatory for large loads interconnecting after 31 December 2025 rather than a bargaining chip, so in Texas the host gives up firmness and gets nothing back for it.
records.microreactor_edge: Nothing here is size-specific on its face, but the 20 MW figure recurs: DOE's ANOPR sets the large-load definition at demand greater than 20 MW, which is the same number as the SGIP generator ceiling. A microreactor-plus-host campus that stays under 20 MW of grid-facing demand sits below the federal large-load line and at or below the small-generator line simultaneously - the only configuration in this whole landscape that is small on both sides of the meter at once. That is the most defensible version of the 'microreactors dodge the queue' claim.

records.what_it_is: In ERCOT the binding process for an on-site generation deal is often the LOAD's interconnection, not the generator's. Separately, Texas SB6 (effective 20 June 2025) requires any existing stand-alone generation resource entering a net-metering arrangement with a new large load to obtain an ERCOT impact study and Texas PUC approval before the load can energize.

records.nuclear_fit: SB6's curtailability mandate is the interesting one for nuclear: a large load that self-supplies from an on-site reactor still has to accept remote curtailment if it interconnects after 31 December 2025, unless it qualifies as a critical load. And a reactor paired with an EXISTING ERCOT generation resource under a net-metering arrangement drags in a PUCT approval that did not exist before mid-2025. Against that, ERCOT's generator side remains the fastest in the country because connect-and-manage studies only local upgrades rather than broad network upgrades, and generators are not allocated transmission costs.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW reactor serving a co-located host is very likely to sit entirely outside the ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Process, because PGRR115 raised the co-located trigger from 20 MW to the flat 75 MW load threshold - a rules change made in 2025 that a 2024-vintage analysis would get exactly backwards. That is a real, dated, numeric advantage: a 20 MW co-located campus that would have been captured under the interim process is now exempt. It disappears the moment the host's own peak demand crosses 75 MW, which most AI data centres do; so the microreactor's ERCOT market is the sub-75 MW host, not the hyperscaler.

records.name: ERCOT connect-and-manage and the Small Generation process (<10 MW)
records.what_it_is: ERCOT is the only US market that does not study broad network upgrades before connecting a generator. It builds the 'driveway' (the interconnection facilities) during the interconnection process and leaves the 'highway' (transmission expansion) to a separate planning process; congestion is then managed in real-time operations rather than pre-empted by upgrades. Deliverability is not guaranteed and the generator is not allocated transmission cost. ERCOT further splits its process at 10 MW: units below that run the Small Generation process under Planning Guide Section 5.4, with the system impact study conducted by the TDSP rather than ERCOT.

records.name: Energy-only (ERIS), reduced-capacity and provisional interconnection service
records.what_it_is: Three related ways to buy less interconnection than your nameplate and get connected sooner and cheaper.
