(2) Order 845 requires transmission providers to let a customer request interconnection service BELOW the facility's full generating capacity, so a 20 MW machine can buy 10 MW of interconnection. (3) Order 845's provisional interconnection service lets a project operate at a restricted level before its network upgrades are finished, under a provisional interconnection agreement.

records.nuclear_fit: Energy-only is a bad trade for a reactor and a good trade for solar, and the asymmetry is worth stating plainly: curtailment is cheap for a plant with zero marginal cost and a 25% capacity factor, and ruinous for a plant with a huge fixed cost and a 90%+ capacity factor whose entire economics assume it runs. Reduced-capacity service, by contrast, is a strong fit - a reactor sized to a host's load can buy interconnection only for the export it actually intends, avoiding deliverability upgrades it will never use. Provisional service is the schedule tool: it lets a licensed, built reactor start selling while the network upgrades finish.
records.microreactor_edge: Reduced-capacity interconnection service is the single cleanest way a 1-20 MW unit can stay inside the small-generator thresholds: a 20 MW machine that requests 2 MW of export interconnection service (with the rest consumed on site) is judged on the 2 MW, which is what puts a synchronous machine back inside the Fast Track door. This is the concrete version of 'export less than you generate'. Energy-only, by contrast, should generally be refused by a microreactor developer - it converts capex savings into an availability risk the business case cannot carry.

records.nuclear_fit: This gap hurts a reactor more than it hurts a battery, because a reactor is a high-capital-factor machine whose economics assume it runs flat out. The reactor's answer is to be the site's baseload rather than its backup — which converts the question from 'what market can I sell into' to 'what load can I serve behind the meter', and is why the diesel-replacement pitch has to be a baseload pitch, not a standby pitch.

records.name: Replacement Generation Interconnection Process (inheriting a retiring unit's Capacity Interconnection Rights)
records.what_it_is: A separate, non-queue process for putting a new resource on the site of a deactivating generator and transferring the retiring unit's Capacity Interconnection Rights (CIRs) to it. CIRs are what let a resource inject at the existing point of interconnection and sell into the capacity auction; without them, a replacement unit would have to re-earn deliverability through the cluster queue. The replacement resource must connect at the same substation and operating voltage and cannot exceed the deactivating facility's maximum generation output. PJM screens for Material Adverse Impact rather than running a full cluster study.
records.who_signs: Replacement interconnection customer <-> PJM / transmission owner, standing in the deactivating generator's shoes
records.asset_owner: third-party developer or the incumbent generator owner
records.term: For the life of the replacement facility
records.price_form: study costs only; no re-earned network upgrade allocation in the normal case

precedents.name: PJM Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT) - the contrasting large-project fast lane
precedents.parties: FERC <-> PJM Interconnection
precedents.size: Up to 10 interconnection requests per calendar year, minimum 250 MW unforced capacity each
precedents.note: Accepted by FERC in June 2026, effective 31 July 2026, sunsetting end-2027. Selected projects must execute a Generation Interconnection Agreement within 10 months of submission and be operational within three years, and must carry a state-authority commitment to expedite siting. The 250 MW UCAP floor excludes every microreactor and most SMRs outright.

records.nuclear_fit: This is the legal plumbing behind coal-to-nuclear: a reactor replacing a retiring coal unit at the same substation and voltage inherits the CIRs and skips the cluster. It fits nuclear better than it fits anything intermittent, because CIRs are capacity rights and a reactor can actually deliver against them at high capacity factor. The binding constraint is the MW cap - the replacement cannot exceed the deactivating unit's output - plus the multi-year gap between when the coal unit deactivates and when a reactor could be licensed and built, during which the site's CIRs must be held.
records.microreactor_edge: Two things flip. First, the MW cap is never binding for a 1-20 MW unit replacing a 300-600 MW coal unit - the constraint becomes 'you may only use a fraction of what is there', which argues for a multi-unit fleet at one retired site. Second, and against the microreactor: PJM's actual fast lane for new capacity, the EIT, has a 250 MW UCAP floor and takes only 10 requests a year, so a small reactor cannot use it at all. The honest reading is that a microreactor's route into PJM is replacement/surplus at an existing site, not any of the expedited new-build tracks.

records.name: Standard FERC large-generator queue (Order 2023 cluster study -> LGIA)
records.what_it_is: The default federal route for any generator above the small-generator threshold. The developer files an interconnection request with the transmission provider, is grouped into an annual cluster, pays a share of a cluster study, then a facilities study, then executes a Large Generator Interconnection Agreement (LGIA) and pays for whatever network upgrades the study assigns. The transmission provider owns and builds the upgrades; the interconnection customer funds them. Order No. 2023 (July 2023, affirmed by Order 2023-A in March 2024) replaced serial first-come-first-served with first-ready-first-served clusters, put hard deadlines on the studies, and made the transmission provider pay penalties for missing them.

records.asset_owner: third-party developer (generator); utility owns the network upgrades
records.term: LGIA runs for the life of the facility; the study-to-agreement process alone is the multi-year part
records.price_form: study deposits + 100% funding of assigned network upgrades (capex, not $/kWh)

precedents.parties: All US transmission providers / all queued generators
precedents.size: 2,061 GW of generation and storage actively in queues at end-2025
precedents.note: Median duration from request to signing an interconnection agreement was well over 3 years; time to commercial operations exceeds 5 years. Of requests submitted 2000-2020, 75% had withdrawn and only 13% of capacity had come online by end-2025. Withdrawal rates exceed 40% even AFTER an IA is signed.

precedents.name: Order No. 2023 study-deadline penalty regime
precedents.parties: FERC <-> all jurisdictional transmission providers
precedents.size: 150-calendar-day cluster study window
precedents.price: $1,000/business day (cluster study), $2,000/business day (restudy, affected-system study), $2,500/business day (facilities study)
precedents.note: Order 2023 also requires 90% site control at the interconnection-request stage and 100% by facilities-study agreement, and sets the LGIA deposit at 20% of estimated network upgrade costs. Study costs are allocated 10-50% per capita and the remainder pro rata by MW.

records.nuclear_fit: Nothing in the LGIP is nuclear-specific: a reactor is a synchronous machine like any thermal plant and enters the same cluster. The mismatch is schedule. A reactor's licensing path (NRC construction permit + operating licence, or a combined licence) runs on its own clock and is not accelerated by holding a queue position, while Order 2023's readiness rules run the other way - 90% site control at request, escalating withdrawal penalties, and a 20%-of-upgrade-cost deposit at LGIA - all of which punish a project that must sit still waiting on a regulator. Firm, dispatchable output is the enabler: a reactor's high capacity factor makes it far more likely to trigger, and be charged for, deliverability-driven network upgrades than an equivalent-MW solar plant.
records.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW unit should never be in this process at all - it falls under the pro forma Small Generator Interconnection Procedures, which apply at 20 MW and below (see sgip-study-process). The real edge is that a factory-built unit's construction schedule (months on site) is decoupled from the queue: unlike a gas plant whose EPC schedule and queue position must be co-managed over years, a microreactor fleet can hold the connection first and drop the machine in later. The claim that a small unit dodges the queue entirely is only true below the SGIP threshold; above 20 MW, an aggregated fleet at one site re-enters the full LGIP.

Aggregating multiple microreactors past 20 MW at one point of interconnection pushes the project out of SGIP and into the full cluster process

records.nuclear_fit: This is the cleanest US template for putting a generator inside a utility's rate base rather than selling its output: the host community signs nothing, pays nothing directly, and the cost is socialised across the whole service territory. That structure would carry a microreactor's capex without a creditworthy offtaker — but 17-0331 also shows the price of admission. The Attorney General's central attack was cost-per-benefit on a $25M asset serving 1,060 customers, and the order's own framing is that '$25 million ... sets the bar for the' benefits the project must show. A reactor at 5-10x that capex faces the same prudence test with a far bigger number, plus a siting question the order never had to reach. Note also that ComEd's existing tariffs 'prohibit the use of customer-owned generation as a source of' supply inside the microgrid — utility ownership was not merely preferred, it was the path of least tariff resistance.
records.microreactor_edge: The Bronzeville footprint is 7 MW of peak load — the exact middle of the 1-20 MW microreactor band, and one unit would replace both the 3 MW of mobile diesel gensets ComEd planned to wheel in for testing and the 7 MW of Phase II controllable generation. A single relocatable unit also collapses the two-phase build (Phase I to satisfy a DOE grant deadline, Phase II for the real microgrid) into one asset.

records.name: Deliberately never interconnecting (fully islanded on-site generation)
records.what_it_is: The host builds generation that is never electrically connected to the utility system. There is no interconnection request, no study, no interconnection agreement, no network upgrade allocation and no RTO relationship at all - the only permits are siting, air and gas/fuel supply. In exchange the host gives up export revenue, capacity payments, ancillary revenue and, critically, grid backup: reserve margin must be self-provided N+1 on site. This has become the default schedule hedge for 2025-2026 data centre builds because the interconnection queue's 5+ year median is incompatible with an 18-36 month build.
records.who_signs: Host <-> on-site power provider (energy services agreement / BOO); NO agreement with any utility or RTO
records.term: 10-20 year energy services agreements
records.price_form: $/kWh or fixed monthly service fee under an energy services agreement

precedents.name: Project Jupiter (Oracle / BorderPlex / Bloom Energy), Dona Ana County, New Mexico
precedents.parties: Oracle + BorderPlex Digital Assets -> Bloom Energy
precedents.size: Up to 2.45 GW of installed fuel cell capacity on a ~1,400-acre, four-building campus
precedents.note: Announced 27 April 2026. The design replaced previously planned gas turbines AND diesel generators with a single islanded microgrid that does not draw from the local utility - Bloom's CEO called it one of the largest islanded microgrid power facilities in the world, and Oracle cited bypassing grid capacity constraints to stabilise the project timeline. NOx cut ~92% versus the gas-turbine plan.

records.nuclear_fit: Islanding removes every interconnection blocker at once and leaves nuclear's own blockers untouched - NRC licensing, security, EPZ - so it does not shorten the critical path, it just stops the grid from lengthening it. The genuine technical problem is the opposite of solar's: a reactor cannot follow a data centre's load swings quickly, so an islanded nuclear microgrid needs storage or a dump load, and it cannot lean on the grid as its N+1. Ohio's Socrates precedent is instructive on what an islanded plant must prove to a siting board even with no interconnection at all.
records.microreactor_edge: This is the route where small size is unambiguously an advantage rather than a rules artefact. An islanded site must self-provide N+1: a single large unit forces you to build a second large unit or a huge battery, whereas a fleet of 1-20 MW units gives you N+1 from unit count - four 5 MW modules for a 15 MW load is a real redundancy plan, one 20 MW module is not. Relocatability also matters here: with no ISA, no capacity rights and no network upgrades sunk into the site, an islanded microreactor has nothing anchoring it when the host's load moves - which is not true of any grid-connected route, where the interconnection rights are often the most valuable thing on site.

Load-following: a reactor cannot chase a data-centre load step without storage or a dump load
Siting/air/water permits still apply, and a siting board can still say no (Oracle withdrew air permit applications for the earlier Project Jupiter microgrid design)

records.name: Distribution-level interconnection under state DER rules (NY SIR, California Rule 21)
records.what_it_is: Below the FERC line, interconnection to a utility's distribution system is governed by state rules, not the SGIP. New York's Standardized Interconnection Requirements cover new distributed generators and energy storage of 5 MW or less; the utility runs preliminary screens, an optional supplemental screening analysis, and if needed a Coordinated Electric System Interconnection Review (CESIR) - a full distribution study - before issuing a standard interconnection contract. California's Rule 21 plays the same role and has begun using Integration Capacity Analysis (hosting capacity) results directly in interconnection decisions. Fees here are two orders of magnitude below transmission-level study costs.
records.who_signs: Applicant <-> distribution utility (New York State Standardized Interconnection Contract; Rule 21 agreement in California)
records.term: Life of the facility
records.price_form: flat application fees plus utility cost for distribution upgrades

records.nuclear_fit: State DER rules were drafted for solar, storage and small CHP and are silent on nuclear, which cuts both ways: there is no nuclear-specific bar, and there is also no place in the forms for a reactor. The operational problem is physical, not legal - distribution feeders are radial and sized for load, and the screens are all load-relative (aggregate generation versus line-section peak or minimum load). A firm machine that runs at night, when the feeder minimum load is lowest, is the worst case for the minimum-load screen. Expect a full CESIR or its equivalent, not a screen pass.
records.microreactor_edge: New York's 5 MW cap and California's distribution rules define the ONLY size at which a reactor is a distribution-level, state-jurisdictional device rather than a transmission-level FERC one - and it is 5 MW, not 20. A sub-5 MW unit in New York is processed for a $750 application fee and a 60-business-day study; the same vendor's 10 MW unit is a different legal object entirely. This is the strongest concrete argument in the whole interconnection landscape for a vendor to offer a 1-5 MW SKU, and it is a rules argument, not an engineering one.
blockers: 5 MW cap in New York (state rules elsewhere vary; the SGIP's 20 MW is the FERC-jurisdictional number, not the state one)

Hosting-capacity limits on a given feeder are fixed by the feeder, so siting is dictated by the distribution system rather than by the host

records.name: SGIP Fast Track Process (screens instead of studies)
records.what_it_is: The fastest federal route: instead of a scoping meeting and three studies, the transmission provider runs a set of technical screens and, if the project passes, must offer an SGIA without further study. The customer pays a flat $500 non-refundable processing fee and gets an initial-review answer within 15 business days. If a screen fails, the customer can buy a supplemental review (deposit = the provider's good-faith cost estimate, results within 30 business days of the deposit) or drop into the full Study Process. Eligibility is set by machine type, MW, line voltage, and distance from the substation.

records.term: SGIA runs for the life of the facility
records.price_form: $500 flat fee; supplemental review at cost

records.nuclear_fit: A nuclear plant is a synchronous machine. That single fact caps Fast Track eligibility at 2 MW 'regardless of location' - the generous 3-5 MW thresholds in the eligibility table are written only for certified inverter-based systems. A reactor coupled to the grid through a certified grid-forming inverter (rather than a directly-coupled synchronous turbine-generator) would be the only way into the higher rows, and no microreactor design has been certified to the SGIP Attachment 3/4 codes and standards. Practically, Fast Track today is a 2 MW door for nuclear.
records.microreactor_edge: This is where the common claim 'a small reactor sits under the interconnection thresholds' is FALSE as usually stated. Under 20 MW gets you the Study Process, not Fast Track. Only a sub-2 MW synchronous unit - or an inverter-coupled unit that has been certified - clears the Fast Track door. The concrete design implication: a microreactor vendor that sells power through a certified inverter and sizes the point-of-interconnection export at or below the line-voltage row it wants (2 MW at 5-15 kV, 4 MW at 30-69 kV) converts a multi-month study into a 15-business-day screen and a $500 fee. That is an interconnection-driven argument for inverter coupling and for exporting less than you generate.

records.nuclear_fit: The SGIP is technology-neutral on its face - it turns on MW, machine type, and line voltage, not fuel. A reactor of 20 MW or less is legally entitled to the Study Process and an SGIA. The catch is that SGIP screens were written around intermittent DER on distribution circuits: the aggregation screen (15% of line-section annual peak load on a radial circuit) and the minimum-load screen (aggregate generation below 100% of line-section minimum load) are load-relative, and a 20 MW machine will blow through both on a typical distribution feeder even though it is nominally 'small'. Expect the Study Process, not a screen pass.
records.microreactor_edge: This is the single most concrete rule-based advantage a 1-20 MW reactor has: the entire fleet size range sits at or under the pro forma SGIP's 20 MW ceiling, so it is entitled to an SGIA and study deposits measured in thousands of dollars rather than a cluster study, a 20%-of-upgrades deposit, and a multi-year queue. The advantage is lost the moment a site aggregates past 20 MW at one point of interconnection - so a 4 x 5 MW campus is an LGIP project while 4 x 5 MW at four separate points of interconnection is four SGIP projects. Note this is the FEDERAL pro forma; individual RTOs and states set their own thresholds.

SGIP screens are relative to line-section peak and minimum load; a 20 MW machine fails the 15% aggregation screen on almost any distribution feeder
The pro forma SGIP is FERC-jurisdictional only; state-jurisdictional distribution interconnection uses state rules with different thresholds
Business-day deadlines bind the customer's return of executed study agreements (15-30 business days) as tightly as they bind the utility

records.name: Municipal joint-action subscription against a published target power price
records.what_it_is: A joint-action agency forms a single-purpose LLC, takes the DOE cost share into it, and then sells subscriptions in the plant's output to its member municipal utilities. Each member commits to a share of capacity and pays its share of cost; the agency publishes a target power price that the subscription is sold against, and members hold off-ramps at defined decision points. This is the only nuclear structure that has ever produced a published, project-specific dollars-per-megawatt-hour figure for a small reactor - and the reason it exists is that municipal boards cannot vote on a subscription without a number. The same transparency is what killed the project.

records.nuclear_fit: Every other nuclear commercial structure hides its price: the Oklo/Equinix letter of intent has its price term redacted, the Eielson award has no published price, PacifiCorp will not disclose its Natrium PPA price, and Dow says only that it expects its cost of energy net of subsidies to be competitive. CFPP is the exception because a joint-action agency's members are public bodies that vote in public. The lesson is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly: the one small-reactor project that published a price could not sell its output at that price.
records.microreactor_edge: The subscription model is a way of assembling many small buyers into one large plant - the opposite of the microreactor thesis, which is to put one small plant next to one buyer. At 1-20 MW there is nothing to subscribe: a single host takes the whole output, so there is no committee, no public vote, and correspondingly no published price. That is precisely why the microreactor sector has no price benchmark and the 300 MW-class sector has exactly one.

records.name: Reservation fee plus right of first refusal and most-favoured-nation pricing, ahead of any PPA
records.what_it_is: A corporate offtaker pays a large cash reservation fee to a pre-revenue developer in exchange for a right of first refusal over a block of future output and a most-favoured-nation pricing guarantee - without signing a PPA, agreeing a price, or naming a site. The fee is not a prepayment for energy: it is returned to the buyer as a discount against future PPA pricing. The buyer is effectively buying an option on capacity and a promise that no later customer gets better terms; the developer is buying non-dilutive cash and a reference customer. Ownership, fuel risk, availability risk and price are all deferred to a PPA that does not yet exist.

records.what_it_is: A customer with on-site generation still pays the utility a monthly fee for standing ready to serve the whole load if the on-site plant trips. Standard standby tariffs were written for intermittent or unreliable on-site generation and give no credit for a resource that is actually firm.

records.name: Price-Anderson financial protection: a mandatory contract term, priced by reactor size in the regulation itself
records.what_it_is: Every NRC power reactor licensee must carry financial protection against public liability, and must sign an indemnity agreement with the Commission. This is not background regulation - it is a term the licensee executes, an insurance premium it pays annually, and a contingent liability it must disclose to lenders and to any offtaker doing diligence. The size of the obligation is set in 10 CFR Part 140 as a step function of reactor size, and the steps are enormous. Crucially, the top tier - a $500 million primary layer plus mandatory participation in the industry retrospective pool - attaches only to reactors rated 100,000 electrical kilowatts or more. Everything smaller sits in a much cheaper regime.

records.nuclear_fit: There is no analogue in a gas or solar contract. A solar developer carries commercial general liability; a reactor licensee signs a federal indemnity agreement, buys a statutorily specified layer of nuclear liability insurance, and - above 100 MWe - accepts a several contingent obligation for other operators' accidents. For an offtaker's diligence this is the clearest example of a term that exists only because the asset is nuclear, and it is one of the few such terms with an exact published dollar amount rather than a qualitative requirement.
records.microreactor_edge: This is the sharpest quantitative 1-20 MW versus 300 MW distinction in the whole file, and it runs in the microreactor's favour by two orders of magnitude. A 300 MWe unit must carry $500,000,000 of primary protection and accept a contingent $158,026,000 retrospective assessment. A 20 MWt microreactor is not in that tier at all: its required protection is the 10 CFR 140.12 formula amount, floored at $4,500,000 and capped at $74,000,000, and it is not assessed the deferred premium because the retrospective plan applies to reactors of 100,000 electrical kilowatts or more. records.name: The obligations a reactor deal must fund that a gas or solar deal never mentions
records.what_it_is: Before a reactor can sell a single MWh it must have funded or committed to a set of obligations with no counterpart in a gas or solar contract: a certified decommissioning fund sized by regulation rather than by engineering, NRC-licensed operators on shift, an armed physical protection programme, and material control and accounting. Each is a cost line an offtaker's diligence will find and a lender will size a reserve against. The decommissioning obligation is the one that does not scale: the 10 CFR 50.75 table sets a floor by using a substituted power level for any reactor below 1200 MWt, so a small reactor is charged as if it were a 1200 MWt one. The NRC has proposed a separate framework, Part 57, that would relieve several of these for microreactors - but it is a proposed rule, not law.

precedents.parties: NRC <-> every power reactor licensee and combined licence applicant
precedents.size: applies to all power reactors regardless of size
precedents.price: In January 1986 dollars: a PWR at or above 3400 MWt must certify $105 million; between 1200 and 3400 MWt the formula is $(75 + 0.0088P) where P is thermal megawatts. THE CRITICAL CLAUSE: 'For a PWR of less than 1200 MWt, use P = 1200 MWt.' So a 20 MWt microreactor certifies the same $85.56 million (1986 dollars) as a 1200 MWt plant - 60 times its thermal rating. For a BWR the formula is $(104 + 0.009P) with the same substitution, giving $114.8 million. The certified amount must then be escalated annually by a factor at least equal to 0.65L + 0.13E + 0.22B, where L and E are Bureau of Labor Statistics labour and energy escalators and B is the waste burial escalator from NUREG-1307.
precedents.note: Two further points that matter commercially. First, the table lists only PWRs and BWRs - a high-temperature gas, sodium-cooled or heat-pipe microreactor is not in it at all, so its amount has to come from a site-specific estimate rather than the table, which removes the certainty the table was meant to provide. Second, 50.75(a) expressly notes that decommissioning funding may also be regulated by FERC or a state PUC with rate jurisdiction, and that the NRC amount is additional to, not a substitute for, those requirements.

precedents.price: No dollar figures. The relief is in obligations, not payments: no emergency planning zone would be defined for a Part 57 facility; force-on-force exercises would not be required; reactor operators could hold a general licence with the facility licensee, not the NRC, administering the initial examination; a general licence would cover certain construction activities before a construction permit is issued for an nth-of-a-kind design; and a single joint application would yield the construction permit and the associated operating licence(s) without further prior notice once construction is found substantially complete.

It says it considered reducing the required financial protection for Part 57 facilities and would instead decide case by case on review of a joint application, using the Act's factors - cost and terms of private insurance; type, size and location; and nature and purpose of the activity - and could likewise consider reduced indemnification fees. So the single largest reactor-specific liability term remains, for now, discretionary and unpriced. This is a PROPOSED rule; nothing in it is in force.

records.nuclear_fit: These are the terms that make a reactor offtake diligence longer than a gas offtake's. A gas plant has a decommissioning obligation measured in demolition cost; a reactor has a federally certified fund whose minimum is set by a table. A solar farm has a fence; a reactor has an armed response force, insider mitigation, vehicle searches and material control and accounting. A CCGT has NERC-qualified operators; a reactor has NRC-licensed operators on shift, and until Part 57 the NRC itself administers the examination. Every one of these is a fixed annual cost that does not shrink with plant size, which is why they dominate a small reactor's operating cost per MWh and are nearly invisible in a large one's.
records.microreactor_edge: The decommissioning rule is the clearest case in US nuclear regulation of a requirement that is size-blind by construction: the instruction to substitute P = 1200 MWt for any smaller PWR means a 20 MWt unit and a 1200 MWt unit certify the identical amount. On plausible microreactor capital costs that certified fund is of the same order as the plant itself, which is a financing problem no 300 MW unit has. Part 57 is the regulator's answer and it is aimed squarely at this scale - no EPZ, no force-on-force, general-licensed operators, a general construction licence for nth-of-a-kind units, one joint application instead of two proceedings - but it is proposed, so every microreactor deal signed today is priced against the Part 50 obligations, not the Part 57 ones.
blockers: 10 CFR 50.75(c)(1) forces a sub-1200 MWt reactor to certify a 1200 MWt reactor's decommissioning amount
The 50.75(c)(1) table covers only PWRs and BWRs, so non-water microreactors fall outside it and must produce a site-specific estimate
Part 57 is a proposed rule published 2026-05-01; it confers nothing on a deal signed now
Part 57 declines to set a reduced Price-Anderson financial protection amount, leaving it to case-by-case NRC discretion
Decommissioning funding may separately be regulated by FERC or a state PUC; the NRC amount is additional, not substitutive

records.name: DOE-authorized test reactor under an Other Transaction Agreement, with no federal money and no NRC licence
records.what_it_is: The developer signs an Other Transaction Agreement with DOE and builds a reactor on its own site with its own capital, authorised under DOE's nuclear safety process rather than an NRC licence. DOE supplies the authorisation pathway (Nuclear Safety Design Agreement, then Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis, then Documented Safety Analysis) and in some cases HALEU fuel; it does not supply construction money. The developer bears 100% of capex and schedule risk in exchange for reaching criticality years earlier than the NRC route allows. A parallel Strategic Partnership Project pathway exists in which a national-lab contractor, not the developer, retains design control.

records.nuclear_fit: This is the one mechanism in this file with no non-nuclear analogue at all - it exists because the Atomic Energy Act gives DOE independent authority to authorise reactors on its own terms, so a developer can bypass the NRC entirely for a test unit. The catch is that a DOE-authorized reactor cannot sell power commercially; it buys schedule, not revenue. The design-control question is the commercial crux: under the SPP pathway the developer hands design control to a lab contractor, which is a very different deal from the OTA pathway.
records.microreactor_edge: Every one of the 11 selected projects is small enough to be built with venture capital rather than project finance - which is the only reason a self-funded, unfunded-by-DOE pathway is usable at all. A 300 MW unit cannot be built on a company balance sheet with no offtake and no federal cost share; a 1-5 MW test unit can. The pathway therefore selects for microreactors by construction, not by policy preference.

records.name: National-laboratory test bed access as a staged, cost-shared entry into operation
records.what_it_is: DOE, through the National Reactor Innovation Center, awards small design-phase grants that buy a developer a slot in a shared, DOE-authorised test facility. The developer still pays for and owns its reactor; DOE supplies the containment structure, the safety-basis process and a fraction of the engineering cost. Awards are staged: a front-end engineering and experiment design phase, then a detailed engineering and experiment planning phase gated on a Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis. It is the cheapest published route from a paper design to a fuelled operating reactor, and the dollar figures are small enough to be startling.

records.nuclear_fit: There is no non-nuclear equivalent because there is no other technology whose first article cannot legally be switched on anywhere. DOME exists to supply the one thing a reactor developer cannot buy commercially: a place where a fuelled reactor may lawfully operate. The awards are tiny relative to reactor capex, which tells you what is actually scarce - not money, but an authorised site.
records.microreactor_edge: DOME's 20 MWth cap is a hard size gate: it is a microreactor facility by design and a 300 MW SMR cannot use it at all. That asymmetry is the single largest schedule advantage a 1-20 MW unit has - it can reach a fuelled, operating first article inside a shared federal containment for single-digit millions of grant support, while a large SMR's only path to a first article is a full NRC construction permit and operating licence on a bespoke site.

A DOME experiment is not a licensed commercial plant and produces no revenue
Slots are scarce and awarded competitively; two developers hold the first campaigns
No published fee schedule for test bed access, so the true developer cost of a DOME campaign is not public
